A library beyond the original

A useful library starts with a promise: a saved page should still be readable tomorrow. The original website can move, change its layout, or close entirely. An archive keeps the words together and gives a reader a quiet place to return. This project fixture is an original text written for Linkbook, with a predictable structure and no dependencies on a changing public website.

The first step is to keep the address and the work in durable storage. A browser can close without taking the job with it. The worker receives only the information it needs, checks the destination, and fetches the document within a bounded budget. A stable record makes these small steps understandable and makes failures visible to the person who saved the page.

Keeping the record

Preservation means keeping a useful version rather than assuming the network will always be available. The reading view uses a deliberately limited document format. Paragraphs carry the story, headings give it structure, and a short list makes the actions easy to follow. Each piece has a known meaning, so the reader does not need to execute the original page.

  • Save the words in a personal archive.
  • Keep headings, paragraphs, and lists readable.
  • Return to the text after the original disappears.
A small archive outlasts a broken link.

After publication the saved version belongs to this archive. Refreshing the reading view asks the database for that version, even when the fixture website has stopped listening. The original remains available as a separate link when it is online. This final paragraph is a marker that confirms the complete article was preserved rather than a truncated preview.

A plain sentence remains safe.
